correct_citation: La Torre, D., Leon, S., Wang, J., & Cai, L. (2019). Long-term outcome study: A longitudinal study of LA's BEST students' persistence and graduation rates (CRESST Report 862). UCLA CRESST. ERIC ED594613.
design: Quasi-experimental; coarsened exact matching at baseline (grade 2) plus Mahalanobis pairing; matching variables included ELA and math achievement, behavior ratings and prior school attendance; multilevel multiple-membership logistic models; controls attended LA's BEST schools in grades 2-5 but never participated
population_location: LAUSD elementary students at LA's BEST schools (two cohorts, grade 2 in 2005-06 and 2006-07), followed to on-time graduation 2016 and 2017; mostly Hispanic, low-income
outcome: Secondary school persistence (dropout) and on-time high school graduation/completion
effect_as_reported: High attenders (>=168 days/yr in grades 3-5) 5 percent less likely to drop out and 6 percent more likely to complete on time than matched never-participants; low attenders had significant negative persistence differences (pooled, cohort 2)
excerpt: higher attenders were five percent less likely to dropout and six percent more likely to complete high school on time than were the matched control students in the same elementary schools who never participated in the program
note: Comparison does adjust for prior achievement and prior attendance. Claim says low attenders got no benefit; report actually finds significant negative persistence differences for low attenders in pooled and cohort 2 samples. "Three-year" = grades 3-5 dosage.

correct_citation: Huang, D., Kim, K. S., Cho, J., Marshall, A., & Perez, P. (2011). Keeping kids in school: A study examining the long-term impact of afterschool enrichment programs on students' high school dropout rates. Journal of Contemporary Issues in Education, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.20355/C58C77
design: Stratified random comparison sample of non-participants matched on school site, grade level, gender, free/reduced lunch, academic performance and LEP status; chi-square tests by participation level and Cox survival analysis
population_location: LA's BEST participants in four LAUSD cohorts (grades 6-9 in 1998-99) followed to 2002-03; 1,224 3+-year participants vs 1,219 matched non-participants
outcome: Dropout from the district database (no longer in database without plausible leave code)
effect_as_reported: 3+-year participants had significantly lower dropout than matched comparison (combined chi-square 8.0 to 13.4, p<.01 to p<.001 across 1999-2003); no difference for 1-year participants; 8th and 9th grade cohorts showed no difference at 3+ years; more participation days lowered dropout hazard (Cox)
excerpt: This study revealed that students who had participated in the program for three or more years had significantly lower dropout rates than the non-participant comparison group.
note: Match included prior academic performance. Size is reported only as chi-square values and a figure, with no percentage-point gap in text. Dropout is likely overstated for both groups (transfers out of district counted). Earlier 2005 CRESST version not checked.

correct_citation: Goerge, R., Cusick, G. R., Wasserman, M., & Gladden, R. M. (2007). After-school programs and academic impact: A study of Chicago's After School Matters (Issue Brief). Chapin Hall Center for Children. ERIC ED496742.
design: Abstract only: longitudinal comparison with similar non-participants; controls for demographics and prior attendance stated explicitly for the school-attendance result
population_location: High school students in underserved Chicago schools offering ASM paid internships
outcome: Class attendance, core course failures, graduation and dropout
effect_as_reported: Students enrolled 3+ semesters and highest-level participants had higher graduation and lower dropout than similar non-participants; sizes not available
excerpt: students who were enrolled in ASM for three or more semesters and those who participated at the highest levels had higher rates of graduation and lower dropout rates than similar students who did not participate in the program
note: Full text was not reachable (no ERIC PDF; Chapin Hall links 404). Direction is confirmed from the ERIC abstract. The regression design for graduation and the effect sizes were not confirmed, and the prior-attendance control is stated only for the attendance outcome. The abstract warns that unobserved selection is not ruled out.

correct_citation: Arcaira, E., Vile, J. D., & Reisner, E. R. (2010, August). Achieving high school graduation: Citizen Schools' youth outcomes in Boston. Policy Studies Associates. NCJ 306636.
design: Matched comparison of former participants with matched nonparticipants (NCJRS abstract); matching variables and baseline equivalence not stated
population_location: Former Citizen Schools (grades 6-8 after-school) participants in Boston, followed through high school
outcome: Enrolling in and completing all four years of high school; top-tier high school persistence; HS attendance; math/ELA
effect_as_reported: Former participants more than three times as likely to enroll and complete all four years of high school as matched comparison students; significantly higher HS attendance
excerpt: Overall, former participants were more than three times as likely to enroll and complete all four years of high school as the matched comparison students.
note: Only the NCJRS abstract was reached (Research Connections PDF link failed with 502; PSA site has no copy). Matching variables, use of BPS records and baseline equivalence on prior achievement were not confirmed. The outcome is described as completing four years of high school, not explicitly four-year graduation.

correct_citation: Huang, D., & Wang, J. (2012). Independent statewide evaluation of ASES and 21st CCLC after school programs: Final report. CRESST/UCLA for the California Department of Education.
note: Given CDE URL returns 404; no ERIC record of the final report (only the Year 2 annual report, ED520524); CRESST site search gave nothing. Whether a dropout/graduation/CAHSEE estimate is reported could not be determined.

correct_citation: Research for Action. (2022, January). Addressing structural barriers to high school graduation: Examining the impacts of the Exito program at Kensington Creative and Performing Arts. Co-produced with Congreso de Latinos Unidos. ERIC ED618050.
design: Propensity score matching of all Exito participants (afterschool and/or case management) to students from the two preceding KCAPA cohorts; matched on gender, race/ethnicity, low income, years enrolled (plus EL, IEP, over-age for 9th entrants); no academic or behavioral baseline data used
population_location: One Philadelphia high school (KCAPA), class of 2020 (entered 2016-17); 75 treatment students in impact analyses
outcome: Graduation, on-track, credits, GPA, school-leaving, attendance, suspensions
effect_as_reported: Participants 15 percentage points more likely to graduate; no significant impact on school-leaving or GPA; attendance about 6 points higher in year 2 only, no significant difference in other years
excerpt: Éxito participants had significantly higher graduation and on-track rates and better credit accumulation compared to matched comparisons, but no significant impacts were found on rates of school-leaving or GPAs
note: The design is described inaccurately. The treatment group is all participants, not only students with early-warning indicators (an EWI subgroup is a separate question). The comparison group is drawn from earlier cohorts, not same-cohort non-participants. The match uses no prior achievement or attendance. The 15-point graduation and null school-leaving results are confirmed.

correct_citation: Alexander, K. P., & Hirsch, B. J. (2012). Marketable job skills for high school students: What we learned from an evaluation of After School Matters. New Directions for Youth Development, 2012(134), 55-63. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.20015 (ERIC EJ973764). Full report Hirsch et al. (2011) not fetched.
design: Experimental evaluation (ASM vs control group) per abstract
population_location: Chicago high school students in ASM paid apprenticeships
outcome: Marketable job skills (mock job interview)
effect_as_reported: No difference in marketable job skills vs control
excerpt: Analysis of quantitative data from a mock job interview revealed that ASM participants did not demonstrate more marketable job skills than youth in the control group.
note: The null job-skill result is confirmed from the 2012 summary abstract. The sample size (about 535) and any school-record outcomes (attendance, grades, credits, graduation) could not be checked: the Wiley full text returned 403 and the 2011 Northwestern report was not found.

correct_citation: Komisarow, S. (2022). Comprehensive support and student success: Can out of school time make a difference? Education Finance and Policy, 17(4), 579-607 (EdWorkingPaper 20-289; ERIC EJ1363229).
design: Oversubscribed admissions lotteries (lottery winners vs losers)
population_location: StudentU, Durham Public Schools, Durham, North Carolina; disadvantaged middle and high school students
outcome: Ninth-grade course credits, GPA, suspension; graduation predicted from an index, not observed
effect_as_reported: Low-baseline lottery winners: +0.82 credits, +0.37 GPA points, 17.1 pp less likely suspended; predicted ~4 pp (5 percent) higher graduation
excerpt: Using an index of early high school outcomes, I predict that lottery winners are around 4 percentage points more likely to graduate from high school than lottery losers (5 percent effect).
note: Graduation is predicted, not observed. Volume/pages not independently checked against the journal.

correct_citation: Mezuk, B., Bondarenko, I., Smith, S., & Tucker, E. (2011). Impact of participating in a policy debate program on academic achievement: Evidence from the Chicago Urban Debate League. Educational Research and Reviews, 6(9), 622-635 (ERIC EJ946282). Related: Anderson, S., & Mezuk, B. (2012). Journal of Adolescence, 35(5), 1225-1235, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2012.04.005.
design: Propensity score matching with multiple imputation on CPS administrative data
population_location: Chicago Public Schools, 1997-2006, N = 9,145
outcome: High school graduation, ACT college-readiness benchmarks, cumulative GPA
effect_as_reported: Debaters more likely to graduate (size not in abstract)
excerpt: Using multiple imputation to account for missing data and selective attrition, and propensity score matching to account for self-selection, we find that debaters were more likely to graduate
note: Only the ERIC abstract was reached; the journal full text was not found. Design, N and direction are confirmed. Whether the match uses prior achievement, whether baseline equivalence is shown, and the effect size are unconfirmed. Secondary lead: Schueler & Larned (EdWP 23-825) describe this study as finding debaters "19% more likely to graduate".

correct_citation: Schueler, B. E., & Larned, K. E. (2025). Interscholastic policy debate promotes critical thinking and college-going: Evidence from Boston Public Schools. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis (ERIC EJ1466576; EdWorkingPaper 23-825).
design: For graduation: one observation per student, linear regression of ever-debater indicator with year fixed effects and covariates including baseline math and ELA achievement, attendance and discipline; SEs clustered by school; alternative comparison groups (excluding non-debaters in debate schools, high-propensity matches)
population_location: Boston Public Schools middle and high school students, schools serving economically disadvantaged students of color
outcome: High school graduation within five years; postsecondary enrollment
effect_as_reported: Debate raised probability of graduating within five years by 12 percentage points (comparison mean 68%), 9 pp with high-propensity comparison; positive and significant in all baseline-ELA quartiles; authors give a conservative bias-adjusted ~5.5 pp
excerpt: we estimate that debate increases the probability of ever graduating from high school within five years by 12 percentage points, from a comparison group mean graduation rate of 68%.
note: Checked against the working-paper version; the published EEPA version may differ. Student fixed effects apply only to test scores; graduation uses covariate adjustment with prior achievement, which is weaker against selection.

correct_citation: Heppen, J. B., Zeiser, K., Holtzman, D. J., O'Cummings, M., Christenson, S., & Pohl, A. (2018). Efficacy of the Check & Connect mentoring program for at-risk general education high school students. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 11(1), 56-82 (ERIC EJ1170313).
design: Randomized trial; mentor for three years starting summer after grade 9
population_location: 553 general-education students with lowest predicted on-time graduation (attendance, behavior, course performance in grades 8-9), large urban district
outcome: Engagement, academic progress, dropping out, graduation
effect_as_reported: No statistically significant impacts on any measure
excerpt: Check & Connect did not have any statistically significant impacts on measures of engagement, academic progress, the likelihood of dropping out, or graduation.
note: Confirmed from the ERIC (author) abstract. The district-records data source was not separately checked.

correct_citation: The listed findings come from Wilson, S. J., Tanner-Smith, E., & Lipsey, M. W. (2011). Dropout prevention and intervention programs: Effects on school completion and dropout among school-aged children and youth. SREE conference abstract, ERIC ED519121. The Campbell review is Wilson, Tanner-Smith, Lipsey, Steinka-Fry & Morrison (2011), Campbell Systematic Reviews 7(1), https://doi.org/10.4073/csr.2011.8.
design: Campbell review: random-effects meta-analysis of experimental/quasi-experimental studies 1985-2010 (152 general-program studies). ED519121: interim meta-regression on studies coded so far
population_location: Primary and secondary school students; international search
outcome: School dropout/completion (and attendance)
effect_as_reported: Campbell: mean OR 1.72 (dropout 21.1% to ~13%); minimal variation across program types; higher implementation quality gives larger effects; baseline-equivalent/adjusted studies give smaller effects; no strong sign of publication bias. ED519121: unpublished and higher-quality studies smaller; attendance monitoring/incentives, child care, community service, school restructuring best
excerpt: Given the minimal variation in effects across program types, the main conclusion from this review is that dropout prevention and intervention programs, regardless of type, will likely be effective if they are implemented well
note: The citation conflates two documents. ERIC ED519121 is the interim SREE abstract, not the Campbell review. The program-type ranking (attendance monitoring, community service and so on) and "unpublished studies smaller" appear only in ED519121. The final Campbell review reports minimal variation by program type and no strong publication bias. Both agree on a positive average effect and implementation quality as a moderator. Vocational programs are not named among the best in either.

correct_citation: Wang, Q., Hsiao, Y.-Y., Hushman, C., & Armstrong, J. (2025; online 2024). The effectiveness of dropout intervention programs among K-12 students: A meta-analysis. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 30(3), 193-223. https://doi.org/10.1080/10824669.2024.2342779 (ERIC EJ1493871).
design: Meta-analysis of 26 empirical studies published 2010-2022 (31 effect sizes)
population_location: K-12 students
outcome: High school completion / dropout prevention
effect_as_reported: Mean ES 0.19 (95% CI 0.10, 0.28); matched and randomized designs larger effects than nonrandom; behavioral 0.33, combined 0.31, academic-only 0.12
excerpt: The average effect size for the dropout intervention programs on increasing high school completion was estimated as 0.19 (95% CI: 0.10, 0.28).
note: The 26 studies, 2010-2022 and 0.19 (0.10-0.28) are confirmed. The share of randomized studies was not found (T&F full text 403). On study quality, matched and randomized designs had larger effects than nonrandom designs. Authors are Wang, Hsiao, Hushman and Armstrong only (no "et al."); issue year is 2025.

correct_citation: Freeman, J., & Simonsen, B. (2015). Examining the impact of policy and practice interventions on high school dropout and school completion rates: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, 85(2), 205-248. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654314554431
design: Systematic review of experimental or quasi-experimental policy and practice intervention research
population_location: High school dropout/completion research
outcome: Dropout and school completion rates
effect_as_reported: Bulk of empirical research focuses on single-component, individual or small-group interventions at high school level; multitiered frameworks suggested
excerpt: Findings indicate that despite research highlighting the need to address multiple risk factors and the need for early intervention, the bulk of current empirical research is focused on single-component, individual, or small group interventions delivered at the high school level.
note: Existence, attribution and design are confirmed from the abstract. Which intervention types showed evidence, and the authors' judgment on evidence quality, were not confirmed (full text not fetched).

correct_citation: Rodriguez-Planas, N. (2012). Longer-term impacts of mentoring, educational services, and learning incentives: Evidence from a randomized trial in the United States. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 4(4), 121-139. https://doi.org/10.1257/app.4.4.121 (working paper IZA DP 4754, 2010).
design: Randomized trial (QOP demonstration, seven US sites, 1995-2001), follow-ups at ages ~19, 21-22, 24-25
population_location: Low-performing disadvantaged high school youth
outcome: High school diploma/GED, postsecondary enrollment, employment
effect_as_reported: Short run +7 pp high school graduation (17.5%), significant; by two years after program and at five years no significant effect, as controls caught up; AEJ abstract says treated youths got diplomas earlier
excerpt: All average positive effects of QOP on high-school completion and post-secondary education enrollment quickly fade away, and five years after the end of the program, QOP has no statistically significant educational or employment impacts on its enrollees.
note: The direction is correct only for the longer-term follow-ups. There was a significant short-run diploma gain at the end of the demonstration (+7 pp), so the result is earlier diplomas with no lasting difference. Details checked in the IZA working-paper version; the AEJ abstract is consistent.

correct_citation: Schirm, A., Stuart, E., & McKie, A. (2006, July). The Quantum Opportunity Program demonstration: Final impacts. Mathematica Policy Research. ERIC ED498110.
design: Random assignment of nearly 1,100 eligible youth to QOP or control at seven sites; final (fourth) survey ~6 years after scheduled graduation
population_location: Seven sites: Cleveland, Fort Worth, Houston, Memphis, Washington DC, Philadelphia, Yakima; at-risk youth entering high school
outcome: High school diploma; diploma or GED
effect_as_reported: No overall increase in diploma or in diploma-or-GED; suggestive benefits for younger enrollees and Cleveland, Philadelphia, DC sites
excerpt: it did not increase the likelihood of graduating from high school with a diploma. It also did not increase the likelihood of completing high school by earning either a diploma or a GED.
note: The given Mathematica URL returns 404; the report was fetched from ERIC ED498110.

correct_citation: Brandeis University Center for Human Resources. (1995, September). Quantum Opportunities Program: A brief on the QOP pilot program. Ford Foundation (ERIC ED420735). The pilot evaluation was designed and conducted by Andrew Hahn; Hahn, Leavitt & Aaron (1994) is a separate report not at this ERIC ID.
design: Pilot comparing QOP participants with a randomly selected control group of peers
population_location: 100 disadvantaged youth from families receiving public assistance, 5 sites (Philadelphia, Oklahoma City, Saginaw, San Antonio, Milwaukee), 1989-1993; net impacts tabulated for four sites
outcome: High school graduation, postsecondary enrollment, dropout, teen parenting
effect_as_reported: 63% of QOP members graduated vs 42% of controls (+21 pp four-site net impact); dropouts 23% vs 50%
excerpt: QOP members are more likely to be high school graduates: 63 percent of QOP members have graduated high school compared to 42 percent of the control group.
note: ERIC ED420735 is a 1995 Brandeis brief with no personal authors, not Hahn, Leavitt & Aaron (1994). Its content supports the substance: random-sample controls, a five-site pilot including Philadelphia, about 100 participants and higher graduation. Cite the brief, or fetch the 1994 report separately.

correct_citation: Curtis, A., & Bandy, T. (2015). The Quantum Opportunities Program: A randomized control evaluation. The Milton S. Eisenhower Foundation. (WWC review, study 82205.)
design: Randomized controlled trial; WWC rating: meets standards without reservations
population_location: 300 students, grades 9-12, five public high schools in Albuquerque NM, Baltimore MD, Boston MA, Milwaukee WI, New Bedford MA
outcome: High school graduation (4 years); college acceptance; final HS GPA
effect_as_reported: Graduation 0.76 vs 0.38 (full sample, 300 students), statistically significant
excerpt: High school graduation Quantum Opportunity Program vs. Business as usual 4 Years Full sample; 300 students 0.76 0.38 Yes
note: Confirmed only from the WWC page, a secondary source; the Eisenhower Foundation report was not found. The WWC page shows no effect size, so g of about 0.99 is unverified. The page oddly labels the domain "statistically significant negative effect" even though graduation favors QOP.

correct_citation: Dynarski, M., Gleason, P., Rangarajan, A., & Wood, R. (1998). Impacts of dropout prevention programs: Final report (School Dropout Demonstration Assistance Program evaluation). Mathematica Policy Research. (WWC study 73966.)
design: Randomized trials of multiple SDDAP programs (WWC reviews: Middle College HS, Twelve Together, accelerated middle schools)
population_location: Grades 8-12; e.g., Seattle (Middle College HS, 394), California 8th graders (Twelve Together, 219), Georgia/Michigan/New Jersey (accelerated middle schools)
outcome: Dropping out, highest grade completed, diploma/GED
effect_as_reported: Mixed: Middle College HS dropout 36% vs 33% n.s.; Twelve Together dropout 8% vs 13% significant; Michigan accelerated middle school dropout 2% vs 9% significant
excerpt: In the Michigan study 2% of accelerated middle school students had dropped out of school two years after entering the program, compared with 9% of control-group students, a statistically significant difference.
note: The primary report was not reachable, so this verdict rests on WWC secondary reviews of the same report. Those show significant dropout reductions for at least two targeted middle-school programs (Twelve Together, Michigan accelerated middle school). A blanket "no significant reduction" does not hold; at most, most programs showed no significant effect.

correct_citation: Mac Iver, M. A. (2011). The challenge of improving urban high school graduation outcomes: Findings from a randomized study of dropout prevention efforts. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 16(3), 167-184 (ERIC EJ934957).
design: 5-year longitudinal randomized study; program facilitator for about 60 program students at each of two urban high schools
population_location: Two urban high schools; at-risk students (ERIC subject: Grade 9); city not named in abstract
outcome: Attendance, on-time promotion, high school completion
effect_as_reported: Nonsignificant effects
excerpt: The article explores reasons for the nonsignificant effects of this program, emphasizing the need for earlier intervention prior to the ninth grade year among at-risk urban students.
note: The design, outcomes and nonsignificant direction are confirmed. Baltimore is not named in the fetched abstract; the full text was not fetched. The abstract calls the role a "facilitator", not a student advocate.

correct_citation: Dee, T., Gibbs, C. R., Margolit-Chan, R., Morrell, L., & Sullivan, J. X. (2026). Unpacking treatment effect heterogeneity in a large-scale dropout prevention experiment (Upjohn Institute Working Paper 26-438). https://doi.org/10.17848/wp26-438 (ERIC ED682795).
design: Randomized controlled trial
population_location: Two urban, disadvantaged school districts; n = 2,528
outcome: High school graduation
effect_as_reported: Overall effects on graduation small and statistically insignificant; notable variation by site and over time
excerpt: While overall effects on graduation rates are small and statistically insignificant, exploratory analyses reveal notable variation by site and over time, mirroring heterogeneity in treatment timing and program implementation.
note: The program is not named in the abstract or ERIC record (ERIC subjects: mentors, tutoring, family involvement, after school), and the PDF returned 403, so the requested program name is unconfirmed. Everything else is confirmed.

correct_citation: Porowski, A., & Passa, A. (2011). The effect of Communities In Schools on high school dropout and graduation rates: Results from a multiyear, school-level quasi-experimental study. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 16(1), 24-37 (ERIC EJ917518).
design: School-level quasi-experiment: 123 CIS high schools vs 123 matched comparison high schools, public-use data, from year before implementation to 3 years after
population_location: Seven states, US high schools
outcome: School-level on-time graduation and dropout rates
effect_as_reported: CIS schools had stronger gains in on-time graduation and greater dropout reductions; considerably stronger with high-fidelity implementation
excerpt: Our analyses showed that CIS high schools made stronger gains in on-time graduation rates, and had greater reductions in dropout rates, than comparison schools over the same period.
note: Confirmed from the author abstract. These are school-level results, not student-level.

correct_citation: Johnson, V. L., Simon, P., & Mun, E.-Y. (2014). A peer-led high school transition program increases graduation rates among Latino males. Journal of Educational Research, 107(3), 186-196 (ERIC EJ1031007).
design: Randomized control trial of Peer Group Connection (12th-grade peer leaders, 9th graders)
population_location: One low-income Mid-Atlantic high school
outcome: Graduation within 4 years
effect_as_reported: Male participants 81% vs 63% graduated within four years, significant
excerpt: male students who participated in the program during Grade 9 were significantly more likely to graduate from high school within 4 years than male students in the control group (81% vs. 63%).
note: Whether the full-sample effect was significant was not confirmed: the abstract reports only the male result, and the full text was not fetched.

correct_citation: Jenner, E., Lass, K., Walsh, S., Demby, H., Leger, R., & Falk, G. (2021, March). Effects of a cross-age peer mentoring program within a randomized controlled trial. The Policy & Research Group (i3 evaluation of PGC-HS; WWC study 90321).
design: Randomized controlled trial (1,351 ninth graders analyzed; 1,532 initially randomized in six schools); ITT and CACE
population_location: Six (analytic five) rural public high schools in North Carolina, ninth grade
outcome: Days attended, credits earned, weighted GPA, promotion to 10th grade, discipline, noncognitive outcomes
effect_as_reported: ITT: no significant effect on days attended (166.33 vs 165.73), promotion (88 vs 89), credits (7.28 vs 7.27), GPA (2.71 vs 2.63); significant ITT reduction in suspensions (5 points, p=.020); CACE showed GPA +0.15 for compliers
excerpt: the opportunity to participate in PGC-HS did not have a statistically discernible effect on academic achievement and most noncognitive outcomes at the end of the ninth-grade year
note: The null result holds for the four listed outcomes. There were significant ITT effects on suspensions, school attachment and degree expectations, and complier (CACE) effects on GPA, so "no significant effects" should be limited to those four outcomes.

correct_citation: Bos, J. M., Graczewski, C., Dhillon, S., Auchstetter, A., Cassasanto-Ferro, J., & Kitmitto, S. (2022). Building Assets and Reducing Risks (BARR) I3 scale-up evaluation: Final report. American Institutes for Research (ERIC ED622608).
design: School-randomized wait-list trial, three cohorts 2017-18 to 2019-20, first-year impacts
population_location: 66 schools in 12 states and DC; 21,529 ninth graders
outcome: Passing all core courses, core credits earned, GPA, PSAT, chronic absence, suspension, persistence to 10th grade
effect_as_reported: Passed all core courses 80.2% vs 74.4% (ES 0.21); chronic absence 19% vs 22% (ES -0.11); suspension and persistence to 10th grade not significant
excerpt: Assignment to BARR caused a negative (favorable) impact on the percentage of students who were chronically absent but did not have a statistically significant impact on suspension rates or persistence to 10th grade across the combined cohorts.
note: Graduation is not an outcome; it appears only as a school-level baseline characteristic. Effects were concentrated in cohorts 2 and 3.
